title: Brunello & Chianti Vintages Explained
quiz.0.question: What is the root cause of vintage differences between Brunello di Montalcino and Chianti Classico?
quiz.0.options.1: Microclimate differences from elevation, exposure and site
quiz.0.explanation: Both use Sangiovese, but Montalcino's isolated hill creates a distinctive microclimate (maritime influence + varied elevations) that behaves quite differently from the rolling hills of Chianti Classico.
quiz.1.question: What did the 2015 vintage have in common for Brunello and Chianti Classico?
quiz.1.options.1: Warm and ripe, concentrated fruit yet still balanced
quiz.1.options.3: Very low yields causing prices to soar
quiz.1.explanation: In 2015 all of Tuscany was warm and sunny; both Brunello and Chianti Classico show ripe fruit and round tannins, making it one of the most widely praised recent vintages.
quiz.2.question: In Chianti Classico, how does Gran Selezione perform in difficult vintages (such as 2014)?
quiz.2.options.0: Still top quality, unaffected by vintage
quiz.2.options.1: Strict selection keeps it better than basic Classico, but quality clearly suffers
quiz.2.options.3: Production stops entirely until the next vintage
quiz.2.explanation: Gran Selezione's strict selection (estate vineyards only, usually the best sites) means it mostly still outperforms basic Classico in difficult years, but overall quality is still clearly affected by the vintage, and some estates choose not to make it at all.
quiz.3.question: What characterises the 2010 Brunello vintage?
quiz.3.options.0: Early maturing and easy, now at its peak
quiz.3.options.1: Great structure and tight tannins, needing longer ageing
quiz.3.options.2: Light and elegant, entering its drinking window
quiz.3.options.3: Affected by the weather, an unremarkable showing
quiz.3.explanation: Many critics rate 2010 Brunello as the greatest recent vintage: perfect weather created powerful structure and tight tannins, with ageing potential of over 40 years, and it is still developing.

slides.2.title: Why Brunello and Chianti Classico Vintages Differ
slides.2.content:
Both are based on Sangiovese — so why do Brunello and Chianti Classico perform so differently in the same vintage? The root cause is differences in landform and microclimate.

Brunello di Montalcino

  • Landform: an isolated hill, with sites facing many directions
  • Elevation: 250-600 m, with marked variation
  • Climate influence: moderated by the Mediterranean
  • Sangiovese: Brunello clones, thick-skinned with firm tannins
  • Ageing rules: Riserva requires 6 years
  • Vintage variation: elevation matters greatly (north vs south slopes)
  • Strong years: 2010, 2015, 2016
  • Challenging years: 2014, 2002

Chianti Classico

  • Landform: rolling hills between Siena and Florence
  • Elevation: 250-700 m, highly varied
  • Climate influence: stronger continental influence
  • Sangiovese: many clones, varied styles
  • Ageing rules: Gran Selezione requires 30 months
  • Vintage variation: differences between northern and southern villages (Greve/Castelnuovo)
  • Strong years: 2015, 2016, 2019
  • Challenging years: 2014, 2017 (drought)
slides.3.title: Brunello Vintage Ratings 2000-2021
slides.3.content:
Because Brunello must age for a long time by law (at least 5 years, Riserva 6), buying decisions by vintage need to be planned 5-10 years ahead.

★★★★★
2010: an epic vintage — perfect structure + tight tannins, ageing potential 40-50 years, still developing
★★★★★
2016: a legendary vintage — fresh acidity + rich fruit, a perfect fusion of elegance and power, potential 35-45 years
★★★★
2015: warm and ripe — concentrated fruit, round tannins, a modern style with broad appeal, relatively early maturing, potential 25-35 years
★★★★
2019: excellent balance — aromatic, complete structure, a wide drinking window, potential 20-30 years
★★★
2012, 2018: 2012 was warm with generous fruit; 2018 was cool and rainy with a lighter style — choose producers carefully for both
★★
2014: a disastrous rainy year — yields cut sharply; only top producers' selected sites made fine wines, so assess carefully
slides.4.title: Chianti Classico Vintage Ratings 2000-2021
slides.4.content:
Chianti Classico vintage ratings: in most vintages Gran Selezione usually outperforms the basic Classico and Riserva tiers.

★★★★★
2015: the best in recent times — ripe fruit + balanced acidity, excellent at every tier, already drinking, potential 15-25 years
★★★★★
2016: a legendary vintage — a cool autumn gave refined structure, Gran Selezione especially outstanding, potential 20-30 years
★★★★
2019: excellent balance — aromatic, fine tannins, good value, with fine wines even at Classico level
★★★★
2013: an elegant vintage — a cool climate gave high acidity and lower sugar, suited to traditionalists, with brilliant Gran Selezione
★★★
2017, 2020: warm vintages — 2017 was hot and dry with sharply reduced yields; 2020 has generous, easy-drinking fruit, and Gran Selezione still has complexity
★★
2014: rainy and difficult — strictly selected Gran Selezione still produced fine wines; basic Classico quality was inconsistent
slides.5.title: 2015 vs 2016: Vintage Character Compared
slides.5.content:
In Tuscany both 2015 and 2016 are outstanding vintages, but their styles differ markedly; understanding the difference helps buying decisions.

The 2015 vintage (Brunello & Chianti)

  • Climate: warm and dry, perfectly sunny
  • Fruit: ripe and concentrated, mainly black berries
  • Acidity: medium, round and smooth
  • Tannins: ripe and round, a modern style
  • Now: in its drinking window, open on the palate
  • Best for: modern-style lovers, drinking within 5-15 years
  • Examples: Biondi-Santi 2015, Antinori Badia 2015

The 2016 vintage (Brunello & Chianti)

  • Climate: balanced, with a cool, extended autumn
  • Fruit: rich yet refined, red and black fruit together
  • Acidity: higher, fresh and balanced
  • Tannins: abundant and fine, with strong structure
  • Now: partly closed, needs patience or decanting
  • Best for: traditionalists, drinking in 10-30 years
  • Examples: Poggio di Sotto 2016, Fontodi 2016

slides.7.title: Key Takeaways
slides.7.points.0: Brunello and Chianti Classico both use Sangiovese, but differences in landform and microclimate give completely different vintage results
slides.7.points.1: Brunello's greatest vintages: 2010 (epic structure) and 2016 (elegant legend), both with ageing potential over 35 years
slides.7.points.2: Chianti Classico's best vintages: 2015 (ripe and balanced) and 2016 (refined legend), with Gran Selezione most outstanding
slides.7.points.3: The 2015 vintage: warm and ripe, concentrated round fruit, relatively early maturing, the modernist's choice, best within 5-15 years
slides.7.points.4: The 2016 vintage: balanced and refined, fresh acidity, strong structure, longer ageing potential, the traditionalist's choice
slides.7.points.5: The 2014 vintage: rainy and difficult; Brunello yields were cut sharply, while Chianti Classico Gran Selezione remained reliable
slides.7.points.6: Because of Brunello's long ageing rules, buying decisions by vintage need to be planned 5-10 years ahead
slides.7.points.7: Chianti Classico Gran Selezione is more strictly selected in difficult years and usually relatively more reliable
slides.7.points.8: Buying strategy: for Brunello prioritise top vintages (2010/2016); for value in Chianti Classico choose 2019/2015

slides.8.questions.2.options.0: Still top quality, completely unaffected by vintage

slides.8.questions.3.question: What is the biggest stylistic difference between the 2015 and 2016 vintages in Tuscany?
slides.8.questions.3.options.0: 2015 is more elegant and taut, 2016 riper and rounder
slides.8.questions.3.options.1: 2015 is ripe, modern and easy; 2016 is balanced and refined with longer ageing potential
slides.8.questions.3.options.3: 2015 has far greater ageing potential than 2016
slides.8.questions.3.explanation: 2015 is warm and ripe, relatively early maturing and easy to drink; 2016 is balanced and refined, with higher acidity, stronger structure and greater ageing potential than 2015 — the traditionalist's choice.
slides.8.questions.4.question: How is the 2014 vintage rated in Brunello, and what was the main cause?
slides.8.questions.4.options.1: Four-star good vintage, slightly below average
slides.8.questions.4.options.2: Two-star difficult vintage: persistent heavy autumn rain caused rot and dilution
slides.8.questions.4.options.3: One-star disaster, not worth buying at all
slides.8.questions.4.explanation: Continuous heavy rain in the autumn of 2014 made it a disastrous year in Tuscany; Brunello yields were cut sharply and quality varied hugely, so wines from top producers' selected sites must be chosen with great care.
